Stage 2 — A hybrid digital twin of a gas-stirred ladle¶

Vamsi Gudipati

The second stage puts POD to work on an industrial question: reconstructing the full temperature field of a gas-stirred steel ladle from 16 thermocouples and the gas-flow reading. An analytic generator (ladle_v2.py, next to this notebook) stands in for plant or CFD data, with six independent physical drivers and a late abnormal double-plume regime. On an 8-mode POD basis I compare a physics core fed with the known inputs, the same core corrected by a residual learned from the sensors (the hybrid twin), a pure-data soft sensor (sensors → POD coefficients, the data-driven route of Stage 1 with sensors as inputs) and a small neural network, then check the plant KPIs and a guard that flags fields the basis cannot represent. I added a training animation, printed KPI values and three-seed repeats; Stage 3 stresses the sensors and the guard.

Portfolio page: https://vamsigudipati.github.io/rom-ladle-digital-twin.html

The Ladle Digital Twin¶

the whole toolkit, applied to one industrial problem¶

In earlier projects I built PINNs (forward and inverse) and a DeepONet, used residual learning, and in Stage 1 two flavours of reduced-order model (POD, intrusive and non-intrusive). This capstone puts them to work on a single, real problem: a soft sensor / digital twin for a gas-stirred metallurgical ladle.

The thread that ties this work together, in one line: physics gives the structure, data fills the gap, and today every tool you learned is a component of one working system.

How to run¶

Top to bottom, ~2–3 minutes on a CPU; dense but every cell is short. Two lines are left to write live (boxed). ladle_v2.py sits next to this notebook, it is our stand-in for CFD/plant data; you never read it.

The build: (1) see the data, (2) compress it with POD, (3) a fast physics core, (4) correct it by residual learning → a hybrid twin, (5) the soft sensor as a non-intrusive ROM, (6) industrial KPIs, (7) a trust guard, (8) the method map, where every method fits.

In [3]:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from ladle_v2 import generate, volume_weights, temperature   # our plant/CFD stand-in

CORAL, STEEL, GREEN, GRAY, INK = "#D24726", "#2E5E8C", "#5E9A3F", "#9AA3B0", "#1A1F2E"
def heat(ax, F, title="", cmap="inferno", vmin=None, vmax=None):
    im = ax.imshow(F, origin="lower", extent=[0,1,0,1], aspect="auto", cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.02)
    return im

1. The industrial problem¶

A porous plug bubbles argon through the bottom of a ladle of molten steel. The plume stirs the bath, loses heat to the refractory walls, and opens an eye in the slag on top. The operator needs the full temperature field, for refractory wear, for the slag eye, for the tap temperature, but you cannot probe 1600 °C metal everywhere. You get a few thermocouples and the gas-flow reading, on a bath that drifts heat to heat and occasionally does something abnormal.

Goal: a twin that turns those few numbers into the whole field, the KPIs that drive decisions, and a warning when it should not be trusted.

In [4]:
g, F, reg, lat = generate()                 # F:(n,nz,nr) fields; reg: regime; lat: the hidden drivers
nz, nr, R, H = g["nz"], g["nr"], g["R"], g["H"]
r, z, Rg, Zg = g["r"], g["z"], g["Rg"], g["Zg"]
wg = volume_weights(g)                        # cell volumes (round ladle: 2*pi*r*dr*dz)
print("fields:", F.shape, " regimes:", dict(zip(*np.unique(reg, return_counts=True))))
print(f"bath ~1873 K; the informative *variation* is only ~{(F - F.mean(0)).std():.0f} K : that is what a twin must recover.")

fields: (620, 96, 64)  regimes: {np.str_('double'): np.int64(120), np.str_('single'): np.int64(500)}
bath ~1873 K; the informative *variation* is only ~13 K : that is what a twin must recover.

See the data : a few heats¶

In [5]:
idx = np.linspace(0, 460, 5).astype(int)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 2.8))
for a, i in zip(ax, idx): 
    heat(a, F[i], f"heat #{i}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Anatomy of the field : six hidden drivers¶

The field is not random: it is the sum of six physical effects, each drifting on its own. Here is what each one does to the temperature (K, against a nominal heat). This is why the problem is genuinely six-dimensional, and why one sensor can never stand in for the rest.

In [6]:
nom = lat[:300].mean(0)        
                       # a nominal heat
names = ["gas flow Q", "wall cooling", "slag depth", "stratification", "swirl", "fill level"]
highs = {0: 1.1e-3, 1: -150, 2: 0.85, 3: 30, 4: 15, 5: 0.9}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(16, 2.7))
for k, nm in enumerate(names):
    p = nom.copy()
    p[k] = highs[k]
    d = temperature(g, tuple(p)) - temperature(g, tuple(nom))
    m = np.abs(d).max()
    heat(ax[k], d, nm, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-m, vmax=m)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Read-off. Gas flow makes the cool plume column; wall cooling makes the boundary layers; slag caps the top; stratification tilts hot-bottom to cool-top; swirl breaks the symmetry; fill moves the surface. Six independent footprints, a soft sensor has to disentangle all of them from a handful of probes.

Normal vs abnormal, and plant-time drift¶

In [7]:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(14, 2.8))
heat(ax[0], F[np.where(reg=="single")[0][20]] - F.mean(0), "normal (single plume)", cmap="RdBu_r")
heat(ax[1], F[ood[10]] - F.mean(0), "abnormal (double plume)", cmap="RdBu_r")
for a, i in zip(ax[2:], [0, 240, 480]):
    heat(a, F[i], f"plant time #{i}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print("The bath drifts slowly, so we split in TIME (never shuffle) and hold the abnormal regime out entirely.")

The bath drifts slowly, so we split in TIME (never shuffle) and hold the abnormal regime out entirely.

2. Compress the physics with POD the ROM backbone¶

Reminder (Stage 1). POD finds the few spatial patterns $\phi_k$ whose combinations explain almost all the variation, so any field is its mean plus a few coefficients: $$T(r,z) \approx \bar T(r,z) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} a_k\,\phi_k(r,z).$$ We weight by cell volume : a cell near the round axis represents less metal than one near the wall. This basis is the shared backbone for everything below.

In [8]:
s = np.where(reg == "single")[0]                 # normal regime, in plant-time order
tr, te = s[:300], s[375:]                          # train / test blocks (chronological)
sw = np.sqrt(wg)
Xtr = F[tr].reshape(len(tr), -1)
Tmean = Xtr.mean(0)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd((Xtr - Tmean) * sw[None, :], full_matrices=False)
basis = (Vt / sw[None, :])[:8]                     # 8 modes, back in physical units
energy = np.cumsum(S**2) / (S**2).sum()
print(f"energy: 1 mode {energy[0]:.0%}   4 modes {energy[3]:.0%}   8 modes {energy[7]:.1%}")

def coeffs(fields):                                # project a field onto the modes
    return ((fields.reshape(len(fields), -1) - Tmean) * wg[None, :]) @ basis.T
def relL2(Fhat, Ftrue):                            # % of the field's *variation* we miss
    num = (((Fhat - Ftrue).reshape(len(Ftrue), -1)**2) * wg).sum(1)
    den = (((Ftrue.reshape(len(Ftrue), -1) - Tmean)**2) * wg).sum(1) + 1e-12
    return np.sqrt(num / den)

energy: 1 mode 55%   4 modes 95%   8 modes 99.1%
In [9]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 2.9))
heat(ax[0], Tmean.reshape(nz, nr), "mean")
for k in range(2): 
    heat(ax[k+1], basis[k].reshape(nz, nr), f"mode {k+1}", cmap="RdBu_r")
ax[3].bar(range(1, 9), energy[:8]*100, color=STEEL)
ax[3].bar([1], energy[0]*100, color=CORAL)
ax[3].axhline(99, ls="--", color=GRAY)
ax[3].set(title="cumulative energy %", xlabel="modes", ylim=(0, 105))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Read-off. One mode is only ~55 % (the bulk hot/cool contrast); the plume, slag and stratification live in smaller modes, exactly what we care about. So the field lives in 8 numbers. Every method below is a different way to find those 8 numbers.

3. A fast physics core · reduced physics / the intrusive-ROM role¶

In a plant you know two things every second: the gas flow (controller) and the wall temperature (wall thermocouples). Feed those into the physics model, use nominal values for what you cannot see, and you get a fast first guess, the same role an intrusive ROM or a PINN-forward solver plays in a real twin.

In [10]:
def physics_core(idx):                    # analytic field from KNOWN inputs; nominal for the hidden state
    out = []
    for i in idx:
        p = nom.copy()
        p[0] = lat[i, 0]
        p[1] = lat[i, 1]
        p[4] = 0.0   # know Q & wall, swirl unknown -> 0
        out.append(temperature(g, tuple(p)).ravel())
    return np.array(out)
baseTe = physics_core(te)
print(f"physics core alone: {relL2(baseTe.reshape(-1, nz, nr), F[te]).mean():.0%} , right about the plume and walls, blind to the rest")

physics core alone: 33% , right about the plume and walls, blind to the rest
In [11]:
j = 12
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.1))
v = 22
fl = lambda X: X - Tmean.reshape(nz, nr)
heat(ax[0], fl(F[te][j]),            "true structure",        cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-v, vmax=v)
heat(ax[1], fl(baseTe[j].reshape(nz, nr)), "physics core",   cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-v, vmax=v)
heat(ax[2], fl(F[te][j]) - fl(baseTe[j].reshape(nz, nr)), "what physics missed", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-v, vmax=v)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The core nails the plume and the walls but misses the slag, stratification and swirl, the unmeasured state. Do not throw it away: correct it.

4. Residual learning → the hybrid twin · the coupling at the heart of the twin¶

Reminder. Don't model the field from scratch, model what the physics got wrong. Keep the physics core as the backbone and learn only the residual $\;T_{\text{true}} - T_{\text{core}}\;$ from the sensors. The correction is small, low-rank and interpretable, and the physics guarantees a sane field even where data is thin. This is how industrial digital twins are actually built.

In [12]:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
def cell(rr, zz): 
    return int(np.argmin(np.abs(z-zz)))*nr + int(np.argmin(np.abs(r-rr)))
probes = [cell(rr*R, zz*H) for rr in (0.1, 0.9) for zz in np.linspace(0.06, 0.94, 8)]   # two lances
Q = lat[:, 0] / 5e-4
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def read(idx):                              # 16 thermocouples (+2 K noise) + the known gas flow
    tc = F[idx].reshape(len(idx), -1)[:, probes] + rng.normal(0, 2.0, (len(idx), len(probes)))
    return np.column_stack([tc, Q[idx]])

S_tr, S_te = read(tr), read(te)             # fix the sensor draws once, reuse everywhere (fair & reproducible)

baseTr = physics_core(tr)                                        # physics core on the training heats
Rtr = F[tr].reshape(len(tr), -1) - baseTr                       # the residual: what physics missed
Rmean = Rtr.mean(0)
_, _, VtR = np.linalg.svd((Rtr - Rmean) * sw[None, :], full_matrices=False)
basisR = (VtR / sw[None, :])[:8]                                 # a basis for the residual
def rcoef(Rf): 
    return ((Rf - Rmean) * wg[None, :]) @ basisR.T

res_map = Ridge(1.0).fit(S_tr, rcoef(Rtr))                       # sensors -> residual coefficients
hybrid = (baseTe + Rmean + res_map.predict(S_te) @ basisR).reshape(-1, nz, nr)
print(f"physics core:            {relL2(baseTe.reshape(-1,nz,nr), F[te]).mean():.0%}")
print(f"core + learned residual: {relL2(hybrid, F[te]).mean():.0%}   <- the hybrid twin")

physics core:            33%
core + learned residual: 19%   <- the hybrid twin
In [13]:
j = 12
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.0))
vmn, vmx = F[te][j].min(), F[te][j].max()
heat(ax[0], baseTe[j].reshape(nz, nr),            "physics core", vmin=vmn, vmax=vmx)
heat(ax[1], (F[te][j].ravel()-baseTe[j]).reshape(nz,nr), "residual ML learned", cmap="RdBu_r")
heat(ax[2], hybrid[j],                            "hybrid twin",  vmin=vmn, vmax=vmx)
heat(ax[3], hybrid[j]-F[te][j],                   "error (K)",    cmap="RdBu_r")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The correction halved the error (33 % → 19 %), and the network only had to learn a small, physical residual, not the whole field. That is residual learning: let the physics carry what it can, let ML patch the rest. The result is a twin an engineer can defend, because its backbone is physics.

5. The soft sensor, pure data route · non-intrusive ROM¶

There is a second way to reach the field: skip the physics core and learn the map sensors → field coefficients directly, a non-intrusive ROM whose inputs are sensors instead of design parameters. Same tool as Stage 1, new inputs.

In [14]:
A_train = coeffs(F[tr])
# +-- WRITE THIS LIVE (the map from sensors to reduced coordinates) --+
soft = Ridge(1.0).fit(S_tr, A_train)
# +------------------------------------------------------------------+
recon = (Tmean + soft.predict(S_te) @ basis).reshape(-1, nz, nr)
err = relL2(recon, F[te])
rmsK = np.sqrt((((recon - F[te]).reshape(len(te), -1)**2) * wg).sum(1) / wg.sum())
print(f"pure-data soft sensor: {err.mean():.0%}  ({rmsK.mean():.1f} K RMS)")

pure-data soft sensor: 19%  (4.5 K RMS)

Two routes, same accuracy (~19 %): the hybrid twin (physics + small residual, interpretable and robust) and the pure non-intrusive ROM (simpler, no physics model needed). Choose by how much you trust your physics and how much you must justify the answer. That choice, not a leaderboard, is the engineering.

Would a neural network beat the linear map?¶

Animation hook. The training loop calls ex_loop_hook(net) after each optimiser step (one extra call; nothing else in the loop changes). Every 25 steps it stores the full-batch training loss, the test relative error and the reconstructed field of test heat 12 for the training animation, and every 150 steps it writes a checkpoint of the network to the models folder. The hook only evaluates the network (no gradients, no random numbers), so the training is unchanged.

In [15]:
from pathlib import Path
EX_CKPT = MODELS_DIR / "checkpoints"; EX_CKPT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
anim_snaps, anim_losses, ex_step = [], [], [0]
def ex_loop_hook(model):
    ex_step[0] += 1; k = ex_step[0]
    if k % 25 and k != 1: return
    with torch.no_grad():
        anim_losses.append((k, float(nn.MSELoss()(model(Xt), Yt))))
        pr = sy.inverse_transform(model(Xi).numpy())
    fields = (Tmean + pr @ basis).reshape(-1, nz, nr)
    anim_snaps.append(dict(step=k, field=fields[12], err=float(relL2(fields, F[te]).mean()), loss=list(anim_losses)))
    if k % 150 == 0: torch.save(model.state_dict(), EX_CKPT / f"soft_sensor_step{k:04d}.pth")
In [16]:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
torch.manual_seed(0)
Xtr, Xte, Ytr = S_tr, S_te, coeffs(F[tr])
sx, sy = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr), StandardScaler().fit(Ytr)
Xt = torch.tensor(sx.transform(Xtr), dtype=torch.float32)
Yt = torch.tensor(sy.transform(Ytr), dtype=torch.float32)
Xi = torch.tensor(sx.transform(Xte), dtype=torch.float32)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(Xtr.shape[1], 64), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(64, 8))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
for _ in range(1500): 
    opt.zero_grad()
    nn.MSELoss()(net(Xt), Yt).backward()
    opt.step(); ex_loop_hook(net)  # animation snapshot every 25 steps, checkpoint every 150
with torch.no_grad(): pred = sy.inverse_transform(net(Xi).numpy())
err_nn = relL2((Tmean + pred @ basis).reshape(-1, nz, nr), F[te]).mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
ax.bar(["linear map", "neural net"], [err.mean()*100, err_nn*100], color=[CORAL, STEEL])
ax.set(ylabel="field error %", title="simple vs complex")
for i, v in enumerate([err.mean()*100, err_nn*100]): ax.text(i, v+0.4, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The network does not beat the linear map, despite far more parameters and no transparency. The sensors-to-coefficients map is nearly linear, so the extra capacity only adds cost and risk. Ship the linear one. Best prediction is the right tool, not the fanciest, the network earns its place only when the map is genuinely nonlinear (Part 8).

6. What the plant actually decides on · industrial KPIs¶

An operator does not act on a temperature field, they act on numbers: bath superheat (tap timing), wall thermal load (refractory life), stratification (mixing quality). A twin is only useful if those survive the reconstruction.

In [17]:
wall_band = (Rg > 0.85*R).ravel()
top = (Zg > 0.8*H).ravel()
bot = (Zg < 0.2*H).ravel()
def kpis(Fs):
    X = Fs.reshape(len(Fs), -1)
    superheat = (X * wg).sum(1)/wg.sum() - 1873.0            # bath superheat (K)
    wall_load = X[:, wall_band].mean(1)                       # near-wall temperature
    strat     = X[:, bot].mean(1) - X[:, top].mean(1)         # bottom-minus-top
    return dict(superheat=superheat, wall_load=wall_load, strat=strat)
Kt, Kp = kpis(F[te]), kpis(recon)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.4))
for a, key, ttl in zip(ax, ["superheat","wall_load","strat"], ["bath superheat (K)","wall load (K)","stratification (K)"]):
    t, p = Kt[key], Kp[key]
    r2 = 1 - ((t-p)**2).sum()/((t-t.mean())**2).sum()
    a.scatter(t, p, s=14, color=STEEL, alpha=0.7)
    lim=[min(t.min(),p.min()), max(t.max(),p.max())]
    a.plot(lim, lim, "--", color=CORAL)
    a.set(title=f"{ttl}\n$R^2$={r2:.2f}", xlabel="true", ylabel="from twin")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Decision-grade. Wall load and superheat come back tightly; stratification is loose, its signal lives near the surface, the region fewest probes see. An honest twin reports which KPIs it can be trusted for.

7. Knowing when not to trust it, the guard¶

The basis was built on the normal regime. Project any new field onto it and read the energy left behind: small means "I recognise this", large means "off the map". A twin that flags its own blind spots is the one an operator will use.

In [18]:
def leftover_energy(fields):
    Xc = fields.reshape(len(fields), -1) - Tmean
    kept = ((Xc * wg[None, :]) @ basis.T) @ basis
    # +-- WRITE THIS LIVE (fraction of energy the basis cannot explain) --+
    return ((Xc - kept)**2 * wg[None, :]).sum(1) / ((Xc**2 * wg[None, :]).sum(1) + 1e-12)
    # +------------------------------------------------------------------+
normal, abnormal = leftover_energy(F[te]), leftover_energy(F[ood])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.scatter(range(len(normal)), normal, s=12, color=STEEL, label="normal")
ax.scatter(range(len(normal), len(normal)+len(abnormal)), abnormal, s=12, color=CORAL, label="abnormal regime")
ax.axhline(np.quantile(normal, 0.99), ls="--", color=GREEN, label="alarm threshold")
ax.set(xlabel="sample (plant time)", ylabel="leftover energy", title="the basis flags what it cannot represent")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"separation: abnormal sits {abnormal.mean()/normal.mean():.0f}x above normal")

separation: abnormal sits 56x above normal

Fail loud, not silent. When the score jumps, hand back to the physics core (which still returns a sane field) and raise a flag. The hybrid design degrades gracefully; a pure black box does not.

8. The whole toolkit, on one problem¶

Everything you learned is a component of this twin. The schematic and table below are the real deliverable of the capstone: a map of which tool to reach for, and when.

In [19]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.2))
ax.axis("off")
def box(x, y, w, h, text, tag, c):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x, y), w, h, fill=True, facecolor="white", edgecolor=c, lw=2))
    ax.text(x+w/2, y+h*0.62, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
    ax.text(x+w/2, y+h*0.22, tag,  ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color=c, style="italic")

box(0.00, 0.62, 0.20, 0.26, "CFD / plant data", "PINN-forward: the physics engine", STEEL)
box(0.00, 0.14, 0.20, 0.26, "known inputs\nQ, wall T", "sensors + controller", GRAY)
box(0.28, 0.62, 0.20, 0.26, "POD basis", "ROM (intrusive/non-intrusive)", CORAL)

for a in [(0.20,0.75,0.28,0.75),(0.20,0.27,0.28,0.27),(0.48,0.75,0.56,0.55),
          (0.48,0.27,0.56,0.45),(0.76,0.51,0.82,0.70),(0.76,0.45,0.82,0.32)]: arrow(*a)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Method Its job in the twin Reach for it when
PINN (forward) the physics engine that produces fields / a differentiable core you have the PDE and need a mesh-free, differentiable simulator
PINN (inverse) the inverse backbone, recover state from sparse data under physics measurements are sparse and you can write a physics residual
DeepONet learn the operator input-function → field, across configs the map must generalise across geometries, BCs or sensor layouts, not on one fixed rig (here a linear map already wins)
Residual learning correct a physics core with a small learned residual → hybrid twin you have a decent-but-biased model and want to keep it auditable
ROM intrusive the fast reduced physics core you have the governing operator and want physics-guaranteed speed
ROM non-intrusive the soft-sensor map, sensors → coefficients you have data pairs and want the simplest thing that ships

Why this is the capstone. A soft sensor is a non-intrusive ROM whose inputs are sensors; a hybrid twin is a physics ROM plus a learned residual; the inverse view is PINN-inverse; the operator view is DeepONet. One industrial problem, and every method you built is a part of it, the point of the whole series in a single picture.

Takeaways

  • Physics gives structure, data fills the gap POD gave 8 numbers; the physics core gave a backbone; ML supplied only the correction.
  • Couple, don't replace. The hybrid twin matched the pure-data model and stayed defensible and graceful under drift.
  • Simple until proven otherwise. A linear map tied the network; the network (and DeepONet) earn their place only when the problem demands them.
  • A twin you can trust reports its KPIs and its blind spots.

Animation — the neural soft sensor learning the field¶

The notebook poses no exercise beyond its two write-it-yourself lines, which are filled in, so I add a training animation. The neural soft sensor (sensors → 8 POD coefficients, Linear(17, 64)–GELU–Linear(64, 8), Adam 3e-3 with weight decay 1e-4, 1,500 full-batch steps, seed 0) is animated from its own training: the hook before it stores, every 25 steps, the training loss, the test relative error and the reconstructed field of test heat 12 (no second training run). The video and its last frame go to the animations folder (02_training_dashboard.mp4, 02_final_frame.png).

In [20]:

true12 = F[te][12]; vmn, vmx = true12.min(), true12.max()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4.2))
def anim_draw(k):
    s_ = snaps[k]
    for a in axes: a.clear()
    m = np.abs(true12 - snaps[-1]["field"]).max() * 1.5
    for a_, F_, ttl, cm, lo, hi in ((axes[0], true12, "true field, test heat 12 (K)", "inferno", vmn, vmx), (axes[1], s_["field"], f"neural soft sensor, step {s_['step']}", "inferno", vmn, vmx),
                                    (axes[2], s_["field"] - true12, "error (K)", "RdBu_r", -m, m)):
        a_.imshow(F_, origin="lower", extent=[0, 1, 0, 1], aspect="auto", cmap=cm, vmin=lo, vmax=hi); a_.set_title(ttl)
    if s_["loss"]: axes[3].semilogy([t[0] for t in s_["loss"]], [t[1] for t in s_["loss"]], label="training MSE (scaled coefficients)")
    axes[3].semilogy([x["step"] for x in snaps[:k + 1]], [x["err"] for x in snaps[:k + 1]], "o-", ms=3, label="test relative error")
    axes[3].axhline(err.mean(), color=CORAL, ls="--", lw=1, label="linear soft sensor")
    axes[3].set_xlim(0, 1500); axes[3].set_ylim(min(min(t[1] for t in snaps[-1]["loss"]), err.mean()) * 0.5, max(2.0, snaps[0]["err"] * 1.2)); axes[3].legend(fontsize=8); axes[3].set_xlabel("optimiser step")
    fig.suptitle("Stage 2 — neural soft sensor for the ladle twin: training"); fig.tight_layout()
anim_draw(len(snaps) - 1); fig.savefig(anim_dir / f"{ANIM_PREFIX}final_frame.png", dpi=100)
FuncAnimation(fig, anim_draw, frames=len(snaps)).save(anim_dir / f"{ANIM_PREFIX}training_dashboard.mp4", writer=FFMpegWriter(fps=8, bitrate=1600), dpi=90)
plt.close(fig); print(f"Animation: {len(snaps)} frames written")

Animation: 61 frames written

What the animation shows. From left to right: the true temperature field of one test heat, the field reconstructed from 16 thermocouples and the gas flow by the neural soft sensor as it trains, the error, and the training loss with the mean test error against the linear soft sensor (dashed) (the notebook's comparison of the two soft sensors, followed through training).

Three-seed repeats and printed KPIs¶

The notebook fixes its random elements with two seeds: the thermocouple noise (default_rng(0) in Section 4, drawn for the training heats, then the test heats) and the network's initial weights (torch.manual_seed(0) in the network cell). I set both to 0, 1 and 2 in turn and recompute every trained result: the hybrid twin (residual map), the linear soft sensor and its KPIs, and the neural soft sensor (the same network and 1,500 steps, without the animation hook). Seed 0 reproduces the notebook's numbers. The basis, the physics core and the guard involve no random draw. I also print the KPI R² values, which the notebook shows only in its figure titles. The seeds_runs.csv and seeds_summary.csv tables go to the exercises results folder.

In [22]:
import pandas as pd
ex_dir = EXERCISES_DIR; ex_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
def kpi_r2(Fhat, Ftrue):
    Kt_, Kp_ = kpis(Ftrue), kpis(Fhat)
    return {k_: float(1 - ((Kt_[k_] - Kp_[k_])**2).sum() / ((Kt_[k_] - Kt_[k_].mean())**2).sum()) for k_ in Kt_}
print("KPI R2 of the notebook's linear soft sensor (Section 6):", {k_: round(v, 3) for k_, v in kpi_r2(recon, F[te]).items()})
seed_rows = []
for seed in (0, 1, 2):
    rng_s = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    def read_s(idx):
        tc = F[idx].reshape(len(idx), -1)[:, probes] + rng_s.normal(0, 2.0, (len(idx), len(probes)))
        return np.column_stack([tc, Q[idx]])
    Str, Ste = read_s(tr), read_s(te)
    hyb = (baseTe + Rmean + Ridge(1.0).fit(Str, rcoef(Rtr)).predict(Ste) @ basisR).reshape(-1, nz, nr)
    rec_s = (Tmean + Ridge(1.0).fit(Str, A_train).predict(Ste) @ basis).reshape(-1, nz, nr)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    sx_s, sy_s = StandardScaler().fit(Str), StandardScaler().fit(coeffs(F[tr]))
    Xt_s = torch.tensor(sx_s.transform(Str), dtype=torch.float32); Yt_s = torch.tensor(sy_s.transform(coeffs(F[tr])), dtype=torch.float32)
    Xi_s = torch.tensor(sx_s.transform(Ste), dtype=torch.float32)
    net_s = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(Str.shape[1], 64), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(64, 8))
    opt_s = torch.optim.Adam(net_s.parameters(), 3e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    for _ in range(1500):
        opt_s.zero_grad(); nn.MSELoss()(net_s(Xt_s), Yt_s).backward(); opt_s.step()
    with torch.no_grad(): pr_s = sy_s.inverse_transform(net_s(Xi_s).numpy())
    nn_s = relL2((Tmean + pr_s @ basis).reshape(-1, nz, nr), F[te]).mean()
    rms_s = np.sqrt((((rec_s - F[te]).reshape(len(te), -1)**2) * wg).sum(1) / wg.sum()).mean()
    r2 = kpi_r2(rec_s, F[te])
    seed_rows.append(dict(seed=seed, physics_core=relL2(baseTe.reshape(-1, nz, nr), F[te]).mean(), hybrid=relL2(hyb, F[te]).mean(), linear_soft_sensor=relL2(rec_s, F[te]).mean(),
                          linear_rms_K=rms_s, neural_soft_sensor=nn_s, **{f"kpi_r2_{k_}": v for k_, v in r2.items()}))
seeds = pd.DataFrame(seed_rows); seeds.to_csv(ex_dir / "seeds_runs.csv", index=False)
summ = seeds.drop(columns="seed").agg(["mean", "std"]).T; summ.to_csv(ex_dir / "seeds_summary.csv")
print(seeds.round(4).to_string()); print(summ.round(4).to_string())
print(f"check, seed 0 against the notebook: hybrid {seeds.hybrid[0]:.4f} (Section 4: {relL2(hybrid, F[te]).mean():.4f}), linear {seeds.linear_soft_sensor[0]:.4f} (Section 5: {err.mean():.4f}), neural {seeds.neural_soft_sensor[0]:.4f} (network cell: {err_nn:.4f})")
print("Result (three seeds): " + "; ".join(f"{c}: {summ.loc[c, 'mean']:.4f} ± {summ.loc[c, 'std']:.4f}" for c in summ.index))
